It solves the performance bottleneck of standard Shear-Warp by avoiding complex 3D acceleration structures like octrees, relying instead on the spatial coherence of medical volume data [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the method solves performance bottlenecks by avoiding complex 3D acceleration structures like octrees and relying on spatial coherence (specifically via RLE compression to skip empty voxels). Source [S1], [S2], and [S3] all explicitly state: 'The algorithm does not make use of any 3D data structure such as octree as suggested in the original paper on Shear-Warp.' They also confirm that the method uses RLE compression to create lists of runs (skipping completely transparent/empty voxels) which 'speeds up rendering drastically.' While the sources attribute the speedup primarily to skipping empty voxels via RLE rather than explicitly citing 'spatial coherence' as the primary mechanism for the Shear-Warp CPU implementation (spatial coherence is mentioned in the context of GPU Ray Marching), the core factual assertions regarding the avoidance of octrees and the reliance on RLE/run-lists to handle data structure and performance are fully supported by the text.

The rendering step is proportional to the number of non-transparent voxels along the rays, which is significantly less than $N$ due to the skipping of transparent runs [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The evidence in all three sources explicitly states that the Shear-Warp implementation uses Run-Length Encoding (RLE) to compress scan lines into runs of completely transparent (empty) and non-transparent voxels. It further states that during rendering, completely transparent runs are ignored/skipped. This skipping mechanism implies that the computational work (rendering step) is proportional only to the non-transparent voxels encountered along the rays, rather than the total number of voxels ($N$), thereby supporting the claim.
